Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data, but their inner workings are not well-understood, making it challenging to interpret their predictions and identify the most relevant input features. Our research delves into explaining the inner workings of a single-layer TCN, focusing on both output and input interpretability. We've discovered that both time and frequency domain filters within TCNs learn to capture both coarse and fine-grained patterns in their input, effectively acting as spectral time-aggregation units. Our findings also reveal that many of these filters are highly comparable to each other, enabling us to create a visual tool for examining and comparing the behaviors of all filters in a TCN, as well as replacing them with a more energy-efficient alternative. Our energy-aware spectrum visualization (EASE) approach outperforms the original TCN models on multiple benchmark datasets in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, achieving a notable 0.3% improvement in accuracy and a 0.7% reduction in FLOPs compared to the baseline.

necessary to perform a large number of tests while controlling the number of false discoveries. The false discovery rate (FDR) control method known as two-stage procedures was proposed to improve the balance between managing false discoveries and maintaining high testing power. The method known as Independent Hypothesis Weighting (IHW) stands out as the most successful procedure in this domain, due to its flexibility in utilizing side information and data-driven decision-making. Although IHW has been applied in various settings, its application in spatial data analysis remains limited, especially when dealing with local dependence structures. The challenge of determining an optimal decision rule that minimizes false discoveries while maximizing testing power is compounded by the need to account for spatial dependencies. The issue of uniqueness of the optimal rule is compounded by the influence of spatial structure on the weights. The development of an accurate FDR estimator is hindered when the dependence structure is not accounted for. The paper addresses these issues by proposing an adaptive version of IHW that guarantees the optimal solution unique and provides consistent FDR estimation for locally dependent data. The adaptive version of IHW is shown to outperform the traditional IHW implementation in various simulation studies.

We introduce a method to generate and study multi-phonon states by converting optical phonons into microwave phonons within a solid-state system, specifically a piezoelectric membrane integrated into a superconducting resonator. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with these quantum-state generation processes and demonstrate that non-classical features such as photon anti-bunching and quantum interference effect are more pronounced in states catalyzed by classical waves compared to their parametrically amplified counterparts. A quantitative analysis of these states is provided through computation of the Mandel Q parameter, the reduced density matrix, and the assemblage of bipartite entanglement. We find that SPCCSs exhibit enhanced non-classicality and entanglement when increasing the initial amplitude of the coherent state used for parasitic catalysis. A comparison is made between the catalysis and the parametric amplification processes for a set of selected parameters.

CT images is a complex task due to the need for 2D images to represent the 3D structure of the organ.  The presence of noise and the varying shapes of tumors further complicate the process.  The lack of large, annotated CT datasets for this purpose has hindered the development of more accurate automated detection systems.  In this study, a deep learning framework based on the U-Net is proposed to address these challenges by segmenting tumors in the esophagus from CT images.  The framework incorporates advanced data augmentation techniques and integrates the Attention Gate and Swin Transformer Block into the U-Net to prioritize relevant image features and reduce noise.  The results from the experimental evaluation using the publicly available VESIC dataset show that the modified U-Net achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.744 and an IoU from 25 highest confidence predictions (IoU@25) of 0.70, outperforming other current methods.  The proposed framework also demonstrated good generalization capabilities when applied to the VESIC test set, with an IoU of 0.737 and an IoU@25 of 0.694.

In its most basic form, the task involves generating multiple types of outputs from a single image, including traditional text-based captions, word-level translations, and visually grounded captions. DC PMM) is a type of memory that combines the high-speed data access capabilities of DRAM with the ability to retain data without power, much like Flash memory. Intended for data center environments, Optane DC PMMs can be utilized in conjunction with DRAM to provide full-speed, persistent RAM.

In this paper, we investigate Optane DC PMMs for the first time as a primary main memory in desktop and laptop computers. Our performance evaluations and energy efficiency assessments are conducted on two types of x86-based systems: one with an Intel Core i7 processor and another with an Intel Core M processor.

Our experiments yield several surprising findings. First, we discovered that data written to Optane DC PMMs is not immediately available for reading due to the memory's write-back architecture, which can be mitigated by enabling write-through mode. Secondly, we observed that power consumption on mobile systems exceeds that of DRAM, limiting the effectiveness of Optane DC PMMs. Third, we found that Optane DC PMMs are not suitable for use in systems powered down frequently, as they degrade over time from the write cycles.

Overall, this paper provides crucial insights into the capabilities and limitations of Optane DC PMMs, which can inform future work in hybrid DRAM-Flash memory systems.

Specifically, we investigate the asymptotic properties of a functional $u_\xi(\gamma )$ that depends on the symmetry of paths $\gamma$. The symbol $\xi$ denotes the syndrome characterizing the disorder, while $\gamma$ represents a path in a high-temperature range. 1. If $\xi$ is symmetric with respect to $\gamma$, the function $u_\xi(\gamma)$ remains constant.

2. If $\xi$ is antisymmetric with respect to $\gamma$, the function $u_\xi(\gamma)$ concentrates strongly, exhibiting a variance that grows logarithmically with the length of $\gamma$.

The framework of no-regret provides the basis for analyzing algorithms that achieve this framework of rationalizability. We present a novel analytical framework for determining whether an game's strategies can yield finite-regret outcomes. We show that strategies within this new framework not only encompass games with finite regret equilibria but also apply to games with finite regret learning algorithms that do not necessarily converge to a Nash equilibrium. We further establish that this framework is both limiting and surjective, allowing us to characterize the capabilities of learning algorithms that result in strategies with finite regret. In an effort to minimize system energy consumption, such nodes must be powered on only when needed, which requires real-time awareness of their power availability.  Unfortunately, storage nodes often suffer from imperfect prognostic capabilities, leading to uncertain performance and, as a result, unexpected failures during periods of inactivity.  This unreliable prediction performance necessitates a careful design of the power-on/ power-off scheduling policy to prevent system over-provisioning.  In this work, we introduce the Energy-Aware Reliable Data Storage Problem, an optimization challenge that seeks to develop a power management policy capable of minimizing the energy consumed by storage nodes while keeping replication factors within safe limits to avoid unexpected data loss.  To tackle this problem, we first assume a Poisson process to model the random failures of storage devices and then propose an optimal scheduling policy that considers the probabilistic prediction of storage node performance.  In addition, an approximate policy is introduced to handle scenarios where the underlying process does not follow the Poisson pattern, and both optimal and approximate policies are validated through both simulated and real-world experiments, which show a considerable improvement in system energy efficiency, although a minor increase in data loss rates may occur.

However, constructing a bipartite adjacency matrix requires matching elements from the two sets, which may not always be done via a natural pairing. In this study, we introduce and analyze a novel variant of bipartite graph theory that accounts for multiple possible arrangements between the two sets of objects, ultimately showing that certain mathematical operations, like taking the square of a bipartite adjacency matrix, can be performed without requiring a natural pairing. This achievement is accomplished by incorporating a concept of "sum over all pairings" and verifying its consistency with other graph-related calculations. Our research confirms the validity of this sum over pairings by linking it to "sum over all walks" formulas and demonstrating that it does not alter the results of certain mathematical calculations, such as those performed with the adjacency matrix. Furthermore, our study reveals that this sum over pairings can be represented as the diagonal elements of another matrix, which has potential implications for various fields, including quantum walks on bipartite graphs.

It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory, serving as essential components in the development of invariants, the exploration of the geometry and topology of the moduli space of knot diagrams, and the investigation of braided categories. There exists a broad range of operations that can transform a knot diagram into a trivial unknot, often yielding values associated with the diagram, such as its geometric crossing number, its minimal representation's crossing number, its algebraic invariant values, and other related metrics. Moreover, the existence of such operations paves the way for the formulation of new invariants, which are defined by the cost, distance, or weight of the shortest sequence required to convert a given knot diagram into a trivial unknot. This study delves into the computation of un-knotting values for all 2-braid knots, along with the identification of local, step-by-step formulas for constructing their projection-based reduced alternating diagrams.

To address this issue, researchers are increasingly turning to models that make it feasible to calculate their density, known as hierarchical and sum-rule models. By leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT, we can efficiently determine the meaning of words in context. Leveraging the AllWords dataset, we convert the comprehensive dataset into a user-friendly format using the Roomba format, which facilitates easy extraction of WSD triples (sentences, disambiguated words, definitions). By training on this cleaned dataset, we can predict the meaning of any word in any text, not just those present in the dictionary. Our experiments demonstrate that FastWSD achieves state-of-the-art results on six standard WSD benchmarks, including a multi-task learning strategy that further boosts performance when combined with other tasks like Word Sense Representation. Notably, our FastWSD model runs on consumer-grade hardware and processes the large Roomba dataset quickly using parallel processing, making it accessible for a wide range of NLP applications beyond WSD. Our code and models are made available to the public on GitHub.

Although a significant amount of research has focused on ordering ordered events, there has been little investigation into unordered events in real-world settings, and no methods have been developed to help agents reason about and sequence such events. uation (WSD) is to determine the most suitable sense for a word with multiple meanings in a particular context.  Although numerous methods have been devised to address this challenge, they often entail constructing dedicated resources that enumerate the different meanings of each word, which can be both time-consuming and costly to create.  A groundbreaking approach is presented here to address WSD without relying on precompiled dictionaries, as it is capable of automatically deriving word meanings from a corpus and contextualizing them within a given passage.  Initially, the method formulates the disambiguation task as a clustering problem, where each word sense is represented by a prototype extracted from a corpus. To validate this approach, a comprehensive evaluation is conducted on the standard SemCor dataset, where the method achieves a Cued Accuracy of 73%, surpassing the established baseline of 66%.  Furthermore, when applied to a more challenging dataset containing mixed sentences, the method delivers a Unified Score of 64%, indicating its effectiveness across a broader range of scenarios.

The challenge of knowledge distillation lies in translating large models into smaller, more deployable versions by training a smaller model to imitate the behavior of its larger counterpart. The problem of providing a plausible rationale for a classification decision has been referred to as the Rationale Problem. The authors introduce the concept of Mutual Rationale Distillation, a novel approach that trains a smaller model to classify tasks by utilizing the same data points that the larger model deems most relevant for its own classification, thereby identifying and learning shared rationale features. The author's approach has been shown to be computationally efficient and produces models with reduced network depth and width, making it suitable for real-time deployment on resource-limited devices.

Our numerical simulations revealed that the drag coefficient in this dynamic scenario is significantly greater than what has been observed in more familiar, static situations. This increased drag is due to the formation of a unique, high-viscosity region, or boundary layer, that forms as a result of rapid stretching and compression of fluid around the cylinder. The stretching causes a layer of thickened fluid to develop, which provides additional resistance to the cylinder's movement. This phenomenon is a significant departure from behavior seen in Newtonian fluids, and understanding it could have important implications for the design and operation of spacecraft and other machines that move through dense fluids.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining its gas properties in a specific region. The area examined is a high-radiation area influenced by a bar and shaped by shear forces. While current methods for distinguishing shapes rely on analyzing polarization patterns induced by surface features, they fall short in accurately identifying objects beyond 100 meters. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model called the Paraxial Maxwell Model (PMM), capable of simulating polarization patterns of electromagnetic waves induced by various geometric parameters, including depth, at long ranges. The model takes into account the effects of the scattering medium, using the paraxial approximation to provide accurate results in the visible light spectrum. Building on this model, we have designed a neural network called the Long-Range Polarization Network (LR-PolNet), which learns to reverse the model to identify geometric parameters from polarization patterns. Trained on Monte Carlo simulations, this network outperforms its shorter-range counterpart in accurately recovering the objects' polarization patterns and geometric parameters from 100 to 1000 meters. As demonstrated through the recovery of spheres, cubes, and ellipsoids, the proposed method achieves high levels of accuracy, correctly identifying ellipsoidal axes within 10% error at 500 meters.

Traditional methods for this purpose rely on physical models or image-based techniques, but they often fail due to the complexity of such models and high computational demands.
Our group has previously introduced a learning-based method in Section 11.2.2 that achieves accurate results but requires a large amount of training data and has limited generalizability.
To address these limitations, in this study, we propose a novel approach that starts with rough segmentations of tissues and works with a smaller training set.
Our new method initially focuses on extracting key features from rough segmentations that represent the deformation patterns of different tissue types.
It then uses a traditional non-rigid registration technique to find an initial approximation that matches these extracted features.
Finally, we perform a targeted refinement of the remaining discrepancies between the start and end images to achieve a more accurate segmentation.
Our experiments on synthetic and real CT images of brain and liver demonstrate that this new method is at least as accurate as the previous method, but significantly faster and much more efficient in terms of computational resources.

Motion trajectory data has become a crucial element in modern driver assistance and automotive applications, emphasizing the need for efficient and accurate methods of estimating scene flow. Traditional approaches to flow estimation utilize optical flow to analyze the movement of objects projected onto a two-dimensional surface, but these techniques may struggle with handling image distortions caused by wide-angle lenses and may result in inaccuracies when dealing with angles larger than ninety degrees. This study introduces spatial-temporal convolutional neural networks (ST-CNNs) as a cutting-edge solution, but also reveals their limitations when working with high-angle projections. This success stems from their universal approximation capabilities, which have been proven mathematically. However, this proof comes with a limitation, as it doesn't guarantee a precise optimal solution to these optimization problems. To address this limitation, we have developed a new proof that demonstrates a significant advantage of AI networks in solving convex optimization problems. Our new proof shows that these networks can provide an exact, optimal solution to convex problems, a notable improvement over the previously known rate of convergence which had a rate of O(1/k) and was not precise. Our new rate of convergence for AI networks is exactly 0, a substantial enhancement. Moreover, this new rate can be calculated with a finite number of training steps and offers a theoretical basis for the efficiency of these networks. We have also established that this new rate is applicable to problems involving mixed integer variables and we have provided an example to illustrate how these networks can exactly solve mixed-integer convex problems. We have also proven that this new rate is the best possible rate of convergence for these networks and that this new rate is also applicable to non-convex problems.

While conventional migration techniques still dominate the field, adaptive multilevel seismic imaging has emerged as a cutting-edge method for imaging the Earth's interior and natural resource exploration. Conventional multilevel methods, however, suffer from limitations such as a lack of error control and convergence issues due to the use of unstructured grids and lack of physics-based multilevel schemes. To address these limitations, we have developed a novel adaptive multilevel imaging method with rigorous error control that overcomes the shortcomings of conventional methods. By integrating adaptive multigrid techniques with high-resolution finite element methods, our new approach provides convergent solvers and a quantitative error estimator for grid refinement. This method has the potential to revolutionize seismic imaging by providing convergent solvers, quantitative error estimators, and grid refinement driven by both imaging and modeling. Our results suggest that our novel method outperforms conventional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, providing significant advancements in our understanding of subsurface structures.

Electrostatic phase plates were developed and assessed for use in an experiment involving the removal of high-energy electrons from an electron beam. The proposed design incorporates multiple stage electrostatic phase plates, each with distinct phase profiles and optimized to minimize the high-energy electron content in the beam. Modern video delivery systems rely on adaptive streaming, which adjusts the video's bitrate to match available bandwidth, ensuring optimal viewing experience. However, the sudden fluctuations in bitrate can make it difficult to identify the highest possible quality available. This problem is compounded by the lack of accurate information regarding the actual maximum resolution offered by these adaptive streaming protocols. In this study, we investigate the impact of bitrate mapping on modern adaptive streaming protocols, analyzing how they affect the achievable peak quality. We then propose a novel protocol, MAXI, which leverages a simple header extension to provide precise, up-to-date information about the highest possible quality offered by a stream. This protocol results in several benefits, including a 10% improvement in task completion for web searches, a 10% increase in content consumption, a 10% increase in active periods, and a 15% increase in peak quality achieved without compromising overall viewing experience.

To address this limitation, we present a context-aware neural synthesis system that incorporates the influence of surrounding sentences, treating past and future sentences as textual features. By extending Chomsky's transformation grammar to apply to previous sentences, our system effectively utilizes historical context. This system performs punctuation insertion and capitalization, and utilizes a sequence-to-sequence model to analyze previous sentences for punctuation and a multi-task attention-based NLP tool to handle capitalization. These systems' outputs inform a punctuation predictor and a capitalization predictor, which help enhance a base graph-structured sequence-to-sequence model. Our results show that utilizing previous sentence context significantly improves punctuation and capitalization insertion, and consequently, speech synthesis PPA and OWSD evaluation scores.

Leveraging both line-by-line analysis and a global approach, we have examined the chemical differences between a sample of $\lambda$ 0-21 cm rest-frame equivalent, L$_{2-10}$>10$^{23}$ erg s$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ AGNs and a control group of galaxies, both lacking any intrinsic emission. mic contraction of developing neurons in the brain. These neurons exhibit involuntary movements known as spontaneous contractions, which have long fascinated biologists. To understand the mechanisms behind these complex systems, spontaneous muscle movements serve as an ideal case study. Previous investigations into the cellular components have uncovered a variety of factors that may contribute to this spontaneous activity, making it difficult to pinpoint the cause without a comprehensive, quantitative analysis of the involved processes. In our study, we employed spontaneous muscle movements as a model system to demonstrate the effectiveness of using objective, quantitative measurements in accurately mapping the processes that give rise to these movements in developing neurons. Specifically, we used objective quantification of the spontaneous muscle movements in Drosophila motor neurons to uncover the presence of a feedback loop that operates within these neurons and controls the timing of these movements. Additionally, we discovered that specific neuromuscular signals play a crucial role in timing these movements by modifying the sensitivity of the spontaneous activity to changes in blood oxygen levels. Our research highlights the importance of using spontaneous muscle movements as a model system to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms behind this complex process, which has implications for further investigations into this fascinating phenomenon.

in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory, designed to accurately measure the magnetic properties of small samples up to 25 milligrams in 1972. 

The core component of this device is a six-turn gradient coil, meticulously crafted and verified to meet precise magnetic standards. These standards include the maximum turn-to-turn spacing, the highest allowable second derivative of the magnetic field, and the lowest possible ratio of these factors. 

A specialized circuit has also been developed to apply a controlled, oscillating current to the tunnel's gradient coil. This circuit uses a feedback system to maintain the required voltage level while minimizing power consumption. 

The apparatus employs the nuclear precession technique to determine the magnetic susceptibility of samples, achieving a stability of at least 0.05 x 10^-6 in the ratio of turning factors. 

Furthermore, a newly created formula allows for the direct calculation of the molar heat content based on the applied magnetic field strength, the oscillating current ratio, and the measured voltage. 

Despite its efficient design, there were certain limitations to the system that needed to be taken into account.

As we advance in our ability to detect terrestrial signatures, the frequency of radio transmissions from potential civilizations becomes a prime target.  However, such signals may vary in amplitude due to factors like rotating bodies and orbital influences, which could be better understood through the study of alien world conditions.  This research utilizes a case study of Gl 581, a seven-planet system, to assess how these signals appear when viewed from various angles and positions on its habitable planets. Although numerous studies have established that VTC processes the semantics of a wide range of stimuli, the area's rich interconnection with both motor and sensory systems suggests its role in semantics extends beyond visual comprehension. To explore this further, we employed high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) while participants performed various tasks involving objects, actions related to those objects, and the sensory properties associated with them. Results showed that the VTC exhibited significant correlations with both actions and sensory properties of objects, in addition to its well-documented relationship with visual representations. Notably, these connections with actions and sensory properties were stronger than the visual one, in line with a comprehensive theory of semantics. Furthermore, these relationships with actions and sensory properties were more pronounced in regions of the VTC that have weaker or no connections with visual inputs, in support of a complementary theory of semantic processing. In contrast, a competitive theory of semantic processing, which posits that visual representations are distinct from other semantic attributes, found little support.

reveal a key mechanism in the formation of neutron stars and black holes. As the innermost regions of collapsing protostars develop high-amplitude pressure waves, they create distinct layers that can either lead to the birth of a neutron star or a black hole. When the first such layer collapses and reaches the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit, it triggers the birth of a neutron star. If this layer is massive enough, however, it will collapse into a black hole. If the formation of a black hole occurs, pressure waves can potentially destroy it and allow for the development of a second hypercompact stable star. If the second star collapses and meets the limit, it will result in the formation of a neutron star. Our results align with the concept of delayed star formation and provide support for the understanding of the delay mechanism in the context of the delayed collapse of the whole star.

The core components of the conversational context are classified into different levels of relevance, which are ranked in order of importance. The theory posits that subsequent utterances typically refer to entities associated with the most highly ranked context components, facilitating a smooth flow of conversation. This study explores the connection between CT and cognitive processing by conducting an eye-tracking experiment on German readers. The experiment measures the time taken for readers' eyes to move across text while tracking the relevance of context components. The results suggest that CT components have a substantive effect on reading processes, with subsequent eye movements being influenced by the rank of the context components. This study's implications suggest that conversations are processed in a top-down manner, with readers using a heuristic to predict the most relevant terms for subsequent discussion.

By analyzing their electronic and magnetic properties using a first-principles approach within a U-type density functional theory framework, we discovered that a critical level of tensile strain can cause a shift from an antiferromagnetic state to a ferromagnetic state in these materials. However, producing ultrahigh-frequency gamma-rays requires extremely energetic protons, which decay rapidly and do not travel far from their source.  If these protons are emitted from galaxies, they may not exceed the "baryon-photon decoupling scale" due to the interaction with photons and decay into gamma-rays within about 100 million light years.  A model based on hadronic radiation was tested using observations of four galaxies, specifically A2744-AB21 and Mrk509, which are well-documented examples of gamma-ray emitters.  Using a model that aligns with existing observations of the gamma-ray spectrum, we found that the density of the environment around the gamma-ray source and the distribution of the protons' energy have a significant impact on the feasibility of hadronic radiation.  Models with a more spread-out proton distribution are less likely to violate the limits set by the number of electrons and protons found in the intergalactic space.  Observations of more distant galaxies may provide a better view of the proton distribution and help us better understand the gamma-ray emission process.

research focuses on lepton flavour non-universality in lepton pair production at high masses within the 2-3 TeV range. To gain a deeper understanding of this topic, we explore its essence through a simplified model, focusing on the interplay between topology and locality within the full Wilson loop spectrum in a two-dimensional lattice model. Specifically, we investigate how these two aspects are interconnected, particularly in scenarios where topology and band dispersion are influenced by distinct periodic potentials. By creating scenarios where these potentials are decoupled, we can isolate and study their respective effects on the Wilson loop spectrum, gaining insight into how topological and dispersive features are represented in this spectrum. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of developing effective algorithms for real-time anomaly detection in data streams in an unsupervised and semi-supervised setting. We propose a novel framework that leverages large amounts of labeled normal data to train a base anomaly detection algorithm in a batch setting, and then adapt it in real-time data streams. While previous studies have shown that certain operations and patterns in base p/q (where the number system uses an integer basis) are achievable, these same features in base p/q (with a rational basis) are proven to be unattainable. Higgs extension to the Standard Model creates a model that can be used to explain several phenomena at the electroweak scale and above. It is important for this model to provide a satisfactory mechanism for electroweak symmetry breaking, generate the observed neutrino masses, and provide a means for the dark matter to persist. We show that the lightest scalar in the Higgs sector can be the dark matter candidate, whose relic abundance is set by its interactions with the electroweak scale particles. We calculate the dark matter relic density using the Standard Model as a reference, and find that the dark matter density is sufficiently large if the electroweak scale particles decay into the dark matter pair. We then consider the effect of the dark matter's interactions within an extended Higgs sector, adding either an inert doublet or a singlet to the original model, and examine the impact of these additions on the dark matter's relic density. Adding such extensions to the model also provides additional means for generating the neutrino masses, typically via a seesaw mechanism, although other options are also available. We then examine the implications of these additions for the dark matter's direct detection and for its signatures at the Large Hadron Collider.

The sharding process divides the database into smaller portions based on a chosen key, which has significant implications for data placement and retrieval. Unfortunately, the default shard key often results in data imbalance, compromising the performance of the distributed system. Although several optimization techniques have been developed to address this issue, most of them focus on shard key selection without considering data redistribution after the key is set or the database is sharded. In this study, we introduce a new approach called BALANCE, an online balancing algorithm designed to maintain optimal data distribution throughout the database's operational lifetime, irrespective of any imbalance caused by the chosen shard key. The BALANCE algorithm redistributes data solely to achieve balance, offering a high degree of flexibility and efficiency. Our in-depth evaluation of the BALANCE algorithm, conducted on a seven-node, production-like MongoDB cluster with a 1 billion transaction dataset, reveals that it outperforms the default configuration by achieving up to 150% better data balance and providing a 20% performance improvement, even when using the default shard key.

However, the process of manually labeling medical images is time-consuming and expensive, especially when dealing with complex multi-class segmentation tasks. This is because different pathologies in 2D images can overlap, making it difficult to obtain accurate labels. In an effort to create high-quality datasets, several annotators often create conflicting labels, which can be seen as an label conflict problem. To address this issue, we developed a segmentation framework called Conflict-Aware Network (CANet) that takes into account the labels' conflicts and their associated probabilities. This framework allows for the use of relatively inexpensive and potentially noisy medical image labels, which are often created independently by multiple annotators. By utilizing a graph attention module, CANet is able to learn the relative importance of each annotator's label, which can then be used to resolve the conflicts and adjust the labels' probabilities. This results in a more accurate medical image segmentation. Our framework was tested on three medical image datasets, including retinal disease, organ location, and tumor segmentation. By utilizing the revised labels, CANet achieved better segmentation performance compared to using the original labels. Moreover, it was found that conflict resolution produced even better results than human consensus labeling in two of the datasets.

While numerous studies have explored feedback effects on system dynamics using minimal models, an underexamined aspect involves the pervasive influence of feedback in complex systems composed of interconnected components. Although traditional feedback concepts apply to systems with self-regulating cycles, interconnected components can also form complex self-regulating structures through mutual interactions. Using the generalized feedback framework, this study reveals the pervasive nature of feedback in a diverse range of complex phenomena, including the emergence of spontaneous patterns in self-organizing systems modeled through the Nagel-Schramm traffic model, the formation of intricate structures in the artificial life game of life, and the source of positive feedback in the mechanism underlying mutual recognition between neurons. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that by identifying self-regulating cycles, the feedback framework can offer new insights into the formation principles of these structures and their impact on system behavior.

In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating a more intricate scenario where LDPC code degrees are interdependent. We establish a generalized probability generating function (PGP) model capable of representing a wide range of interdependent degree distributions, which also encompasses the traditional independent distributions as a specific case. Our study demonstrates that most LDPC codes conforming to our intricate distribution still exhibit reliable performance, close to that of codes with independent distributions. Furthermore, our research reveals a significant issue with independent degree distributions: it often includes an excessive number of high-degree edges, which can negatively impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our intricate distribution mitigates this issue, potentially enhancing the performance of LDPC codes. This discovery suggests that interdependent structure within the LDPC code graph is a crucial factor in determining its performance.

hadron colliders can be established through accurate predictions of parton distribution functions (PDFs) and fragmentation functions (FFs). To make such predictions, the process of global fit is employed to analyze available experimental data from various sources, yielding a set of discrete parametric representations that quantify the associated uncertainties. However, the conventional method of PDF/FF fitting fails to properly account for the covariance between different parton sectors and the correlation of uncertainties across different global fit datasets, resulting in a limitation of uncertainty estimation that can be best represented by a diagonal matrix of semi-gaussian fluctuations. In this study, a novel framework based on the $\chi^2$ minimization principle and paired Monte Carlo simulations is proposed, which not only provides a reliable uncertainty quantification but also captures the necessary correlations between different PDF/FF sets and across different functional shapes. As a demonstration, this new UGLA20 Monte Carlo error framework has been applied to a newly introduced sea and anti-sea parton distribution function based on experimental data from the Drell-Yan process at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV.

Networks (CNNs) have gained significant popularity in video anomaly detection due to their impressive performance. This paper proposes a novel framework called VAScine, which provides a comprehensive and granular assessment of video anomaly detection models under diverse lighting conditions. VAScine provides a detailed analysis of the decision-making processes within anomaly detection models, as well as the impact of different lighting conditions on the models' performance. Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, where multiple radar systems share the same spectrum without causing mutual interference. planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has been explored by scientists. This study presents a more advanced version of the concept, suggesting that life may travel through vast numbers of galaxies, exchanging biological material and genetic information between galaxies. We examined a range of factors, including stellar evolution, supernova explosions, neutron star collisions, black hole formation, galactic star formation rates, gas dynamics, cosmic ray movements, and the internal structure of galaxies, to see how they might influence the journey of life. Our analysis revealed that while certain events could destroy life, there are also routes within galaxies where life could survive for billions of years, traveling from a galaxy's center to its outer edges and back again. To better understand the journey of life, we created a set of equations to track its movement and created computer simulations to see how life would move through different types of galaxies. Our simulations showed that life could travel for hundreds of millions of years within one galaxy, exchanging genetic material with other life forms, before potentially traveling to another galaxy. This process could repeat itself, leading to a form of universal panspermia, where life and genetic information is shared across the entire universe.

We found that panther home ranges varied significantly over time and were influenced by sex, age, and seasonal changes. been proposed to efficiently solve combinatorial optimization problems, particularly those involving the minimization of the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. By mapping problems directly onto the physical system, this approach leverages the target system's fundamental properties. Nevertheless, the annealing process often faces obstructions caused by unsuitable problem parameters, which can significantly hinder its performance. In order to overcome this limitation, we introduce and demonstrate the effectiveness of a new strategy called the quantum annealing with an artificial target Hamiltonian approach. Specifically, this method suggests setting the final Hamiltonian parameters arbitrarily and instead redefining the problem to find an equivalent solution within the annealer's native state space. Instead of struggling with highly excited states directly related to the original Hamiltonian, this approach enables access to the target Hamiltonian's fundamental ground state, thus facilitating smoother quantum evolution. As the fundamental ground state exhibits greater stability, it is less susceptible to small perturbations, thus significantly enhancing the feasibility of quantum annealing. In order to validate this novel strategy, we apply it to the resolution of a 2000-qubit instance of the Graph Partition problem, successfully obtaining a low-energy state closely resembling the optimal solution, whereas direct annealing resulted in a highly excited state far removed from the fundamental ground state.

We investigate how a lack of structured information, specifically in categorization structures, influences search behaviors and outcomes. Using Amazon Mechanical Turk, we conducted three experiments to examine the effect of categorization gaps on search efficiency and the willingness to engage with search tools. The results show that individuals become less effective and less inclined to use search tools when presented with category gaps, which in turn increases their difficulty in finding relevant information. In the case of quantum annealing, starting from a uniform ground state and gradually altering the Hamiltonian to its geographically localized ground-state segments is a key process. In contrast, quenching involves suddenly changing the Hamiltonian from its localized ground-state segments to a uniform ground-state configuration, thereby releasing stored energy. We have developed a model based on the Heisenberg Hamiltonian, incorporating a time-dependent exchange interaction, to study both processes. Our research shows that the stability of the quenching protocol is highly dependent on the initial system state, as it is influenced by both the system's stored energy and the emergence of a dynamic phase. In our numerical simulations, we found that the emergence of a dynamic phase can be prevented or mitigated by releasing stored energy upon sudden annealing. Conversely, introducing stored energy upon sudden quenching from a uniform configuration can be precluded by releasing energy upon gradual quenching from localized ground states. These phenomena can serve as an educational tool to introduce students to the principles of quantum annealing and quenching.

two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, possess a symmetry allowing for a balance between a confining trap and self-stabilizing soliton forces in any spatial dimension. However, models which incorporate quantum gradient terms lack this symmetry and consequently only exist in zero and two or higher-dimensional space. This research reveals that analogous solitons can be formed by substituting the quantum gradient terms with magnetic spin-orbit coupling, enabling the creation of stable Bose-Einstein condensate solitons in any dimensional space, irrespective of the trap's symmetry. This new type of soliton is not limited to one-dimensional line solitons, as it can also exist in two-dimensional and three-dimensional forms. Notably, two or three-dimensional solitons can be created by balancing quantum gradient terms after the replacement, and these solitons are robust against the effects of the mass quantum gradient and can be manipulated to oscillate, expand, or contract dynamically. These properties are advantageous for the manipulation of Bose-Einstein condensate solitons in any spatial dimension.

Electromagnetic Observer (GEO600) is to enhance the sensitivity of the 123m-recycling interferometer while detecting transient electromagnetic radiation sources. GEO600 has successfully identified several types of enhancement cavities that could be utilized in multiple sensing applications. A key feature of the setup is a Power Recirculation Trap which consists of two enhancement cavities that operate with frequencies near resonance. This enhancement configuration has demonstrated the ability to precisely measure the shift in laser wavelength by 0.001pm, at the expense of reducing the main detector's gravitational wave sensitivity. Furthermore, the group has explored the possibility of using the GEO600 enhancement configuration to detect a hypothetical axion dark matter with masses in the range of 2-10 nanoelectronvolts. If axion dark matter is discovered, its presence would result in the conversion of a global oscillating axion field into laser light within the main detector's beam path. In order to contain and amplify this signal, a high-amplification loop has been constructed using the GEO600 Power Recirculation Trap. In theory, this setup could enable the detection of axion dark matter with estimated fluxes as low as 10^{-11} cm^{-2} s^{-1}.

To address this issue, we developed the Game of Lies model, a non-zero sum game that simulates the interaction between the BS and vehicles. However, in two-dimensional quantum Hall bars, the flow of edge currents is limited and constrained by sample boundaries, hindering their application in 2D-based circuitry. In contrast, Ramanathan and Taylor have demonstrated the existence of semi-quantized circulating currents in the gap regions surrounding magnetization domains in a 2D electron gas, constricted by a spiral pattern of gates. These circulating currents are capable of flowing in closed loops, analogous to the paths found in classical circuitry. We have identified the underlying mechanism responsible for these circulating currents, revealing that multiple interference between the Ramyi mode and the skew scattering mode results in enhanced currents within the Ramanathan-Taylor spiral, while simpler gate patterns may lead to currents flowing in reverse directions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the design of spintronics and valleytronics devices based on circulating currents.

However, the hand-crafted nature of LSTM limits its learning capabilities to predefined neural network structures and makes it difficult to integrate with other components in complex systems. The need arises for a breakthrough that can not only model long-term dependencies but also integrate seamlessly with other components in comprehensive systems. This paper introduces Continuous Recurrent Unit (CRU), a novel neural network architecture inspired by LSTM, incorporating both exponential forgetting and splitting mechanisms to manage long-term dependencies effectively. The versatility of CRU makes it adaptable to various complex systems, including those involving multi-modal data, co-occurring events, and diverse task types. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of CRU over LSTM and Long Short-Term Memory networks in various scenarios, with LSTM being outperformed by a significant margin in some cases, highlighting the potential of CRU to set a new benchmark in sequence analysis tasks.

A recent study demonstrated the validity of this conjecture for a specific supergravity theory with a single graviton, applicable to theories with a small number of dimensions and fields, by checking the requirements for charged black holes to exist within these frameworks. This research builds upon that groundwork but delves deeper into the existence conditions for charged black holes and their relevance to the WC. A crucial aspect of the WC is understanding the behavior of extremal black holes upon quantization. Previously, research had indicated the impossibility of satisfying the discharge inequality for certain extremal black holes within a specific parameter range. To address this limitation, this study considers higher-order corrections to the discharge inequality as an alternative. By doing so, it confirms that the discharge inequality can be satisfied for the quantum case of certain extremal black holes, providing a significant advancement in our comprehension of the WC. As a practical application, this approach is used to establish the validity of the WC in specific supergravity theories, including one with parameters $p=2$, $\lambda=1/2$ in four dimensions and another in six dimensions with parameters $p=2$, $\lambda=1/\sqrt{2}$.

Scattering is a common light-matter interaction where incident light is redirected in different directions due to irregularities, and it is responsible for natural occurrences such as the blue sky and the red sunset. Despite its prevalence, much about scattering remains unexplained, prompting ongoing research into its various forms, which can affect the direction, polarization, and wavelength of light.

Solid materials exhibit different scattering patterns due to their complex internal structures, and they can redirect incident light in irregular patterns, linear patterns, and uniform patterns. Different types of scattering exist, including Mie scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and Raman scattering. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of light scattering in solid materials, covering its fundamental principles, practical applications, and ongoing research developments.

Specifically, we examine whether codes based on random single X-type and single Z-type checks can successfully solve the 3-XZ-satisfiability problem. Utilizing the quantum inverse scattering technique, we derive the precise conditions to determine whether a random system of quantum checks is equivalent to a non-trivial quantum phase or can be transformed into a product state. By establishing this connection, we are able to provide conditions to solve 3-XZ-satisfiability using phase-transition phenomena associated with quantum error correcting codes. Using both analytical and numerical approaches, we confirm that the applicable condition for codes constructed from local check matrices is less stringent than the applicable condition for product-state solutions, thereby confirming that random quantum error correcting codes can solve certain instances of 3-XZ-satisfiability that classical product-state solutions cannot.

gamma-ray bursts originating from fast rotating neutron stars was first suggested by Milgrom and Rees. In this study, we re-examined and expanded upon Uzdensky and Thompson's model, conducting a thorough analysis of its current behavior, deriving an analytical expression for the light curve that is consistent with observations. Furthermore, we identified a previously unexplored regime within the model and identified key parameters that dictate the events' durations and energy distributions.

To understand this transition, we've developed a numerical model of the fully convective interior of a solar-type star, incorporating its rotational motion. Utilizing the anelastic approximation, we've observed the emergence of spiral-shaped convection patterns, which are responsible for the alignment of convection rolls along the star's rotation axis. These patterns exhibit the ability to interact with the star's rotation axis, causing precession and causing the alignment to shift. When the convection patterns reach a critical threshold, their tendency to organize along the axis is disrupted, causing the alignment to precess and shift. This, in turn, affects the star's observable properties, such as its magnetic activity, which can be used to track the evolution of its internal structure.

To tackle this subject, we examined how charge impacts the dimerization reaction of NO2-, a process that is significant in atmospheric chemistry and has significant implications in the destruction of the ozone layer. By utilizing a combination of ion mobility-mass spectrometry and theoretical modeling, including classical mechanics and density functional theory, along with Monte Carlo simulations, we explored the dimerization reaction in acetone droplets as they became charged, especially at very low energies. 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda, as well as applications in formal verification of mathematics and computer systems. This paper presents an innovative approach to higher-order constructive real number reasoning by introducing the Constructive Higher-order Real Arithmetix, a theory that allows for the development of significant mathematical theories over real numbers in a programming language setting. Specifically, this theory allows for the derivation of key properties of real numbers, including order, distance inequalities, the completeness property, least upper and greatest lower bounds, and sequences that converge to their limits. These features enable the formulation of important areas of mathematics, including analysis topology and metric space theory. Notably, this theory can be used to verify complex computer-assisted mathematical proofs, including those published in the Fields Medal-winning works of Perelman and De Bruijn.

First-principles calculations were used to explore the impact of N-doping on the electrical conductivity and magnetism in these structures. Our theoretical models demonstrate the potential of N-doped carbon-based nanoribbons to function as spin filters and semi-conducting devices, with implications for the development of next-generation electronic devices.

vin first explored the concept of list chromatic numbers for set systems, which has since become a highly influential and extensively studied topic in the field of combinatorics. Our research aims to advance our understanding of this parameter within the context of tripartite triple systems, which are now the focus of our study. To achieve this, we derive a new upper bound for the chromatic number, specifically, we show that the largest possible size of a set system, composed of tripartite triplets from three given sets, allows for a $\Delta$-list chromatic number not exceeding $O(\Delta^{10})$. continuum cores from the Herschel APEX PREgal survey in the Antlia Carinae star-forming region has been conducted to understand the properties of dense gas at various spatial scales. The study focuses on characterizing the continuum properties, specifically continuum mass and the distribution of continuum sources, and also examines the influence of the column depth distribution on continuum mass estimation. A comparison with CO line data allows us to derive the link between the continuum and gas dynamics within this star-forming region. The study reveals a mean continuum mass of 0.34 solar masses per 0.1 square parsecs, with the mass estimation being heavily dependent on the minimum column depth threshold used. The conversion between continuum mass and the product of the column depth and velocity in the Antlia Carinae region suggests an effective sound cloud of approximately 16.6 solar masses per kiloparsec per kilometer per second, which is indicative of gravitationally unstable clouds in this region. The analysis also shows that the dense gas within this star-forming region may be marginally unable to support gravitational instability on a global scale. Antlia Carinae's dense gas exhibits similar substructure patterns to those found in other well-studied regions in the Milky Way, suggesting a common mechanism for the formation of molecular clouds. The study further highlights the significant impact of the line-of-sight integration on the estimation of continuum mass in this region.

This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures can be transformed into linearly ordered structures by considering their transitive closures, thereby demonstrating that both intuitionistic and Godel modal logics possess prelinearity as a fundamental characteristic. The study further examines how algebraic semantics can be applied to distinguish between logics with diverse interactions between their two modal operators.

Recent research has highlighted the complex role that interface roughness plays in understanding the interplay between surface effects and wall slip during the Darcy–Rayleigh instability in saturated, rough rocks. We investigate this problem numerically, utilizing a non-local slip model and a rigorous representation of the Rayleigh number to account for surface roughness and wall slip simultaneously. Our findings indicate that surface roughness amplifies the influence of wall slip on the onset of convective patterns and the associated Nusselt number. Notably, increased surface roughness can either intensify or mitigate the mitigating effect of wall slip on the Nusselt number. Additionally, wall slip induces a shift from 2-fold to 4-fold symmetry in convective cells, with the extent of this effect varying based on the level of surface roughness.

Complex systems science has made substantial progress in areas such as predicting weather patterns and the trajectory of planetary bodies due to their capacity to simulate and model intricate phenomena. Complex systems have a universal nature, allowing them to model the behavior of any system composed of multiple interacting components. Complex systems can also provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of systems in the real world, such as the spread of diseases, the formation of traffic jams, and the collapse of financial markets. Despite these advantages, the field of complex systems has struggled to gain widespread acceptance due to a lack of standardized testing methods. This paper introduces a novel testing framework that utilizes a meta-system to evaluate the reliability of complex systems models. The meta-system is designed to automatically test the models against a wide range of scenarios and identify discrepancies between the predicted and actual outcomes. This framework can be applied to a wide variety of models, including neural networks, statistical models, and machine learning algorithms. The paper presents the design and implementation of the meta-system and demonstrates its effectiveness through the evaluation of the BaSiL model, which simulates the spread of COVID-19.

To address the growing demand for accountability, we introduce the concept of interpretable essay scoring systems, an extension of previous AES research, and explore the challenges of creating such systems. Specifically, we investigate methods for constructing models that not only perform well but also provide clear and justifiable feedback to users. We explore the challenges of creating such models due to the subjective and multifaceted nature of the task at hand, and we propose a novel, task-specific definition of interpretability that considers both local and global dimensions. AR at the Max-Planck-Institut für Plasmaphysik in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves in a confined device. A key part of this facility is the ion cyclotron resonance chamber which is lined with 16 capacitive antennas that are used to produce and study plasma turbulence. These antennas are an integral part of the facility and have been the subject of detailed analysis to understand the forces acting upon them during experiments. The analysis reveals the distribution of forces across the antennas and their potential impact on understanding plasma behavior. The analysis also highlights the risks posed by strong currents flowing through the antennas and how they can be monitored to prevent damage.

Due to the lack of traditional programming language features, Ethereum's minimal scripting language is intentionally designed for security, with a focus on minimizing vulnerabilities. However, this security-oriented approach also makes it difficult for developers to write bug-free code efficiently. As a result, there is a growing interest in employing assistance tools to facilitate the development process. This study evaluates the applicability of a static analysis tool, SemAnt, in unearthing security flaws in Ethereum's smart contracts. To do this, we created four distinct test cases, which are widely recognized benchmarks in the industry, and modified popular Ethereum-based smart contracts to operate within the analysis's limited input specifications. The results demonstrate that SemAnt can successfully identify four previously unknown security flaws in the test cases, along with numerous additional issues during runtime, such as gas exhaustion and re-entrancy risks. The study's findings also suggest that static analysis has significant potential in detecting and preventing security issues in Ethereum's smart contracts.

gravity can be reformulated as a theory of group elements based on an affine group, specifically $\textrm{SL}(2,\textrm{\xchar R})\textrm{\xchar R}$. By analyzing the thermodynamic behavior using the Bethe ansatz in the large $N$ limit, we find that a phase transition in the chemical potential occurs, transitioning from an extant phase to a confining phase. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the expectation values of certain chiral primary operators and the Wilson loop, and propose that the extant phase in the two-dimensional model corresponds to the Sasaki-Ahnström phase in the higher-spin duality framework.

we apply a variation of Olbers' argument to dark energy, utilizing a constant cosmic density of visible galaxies, the Hubble volume limit, and light from infinite distances reaching us today due to the expanding universe. We then introduce a method to visually confirm the presence and properties of dark energy, involving a precise measurement of a universal average brightness, which serves as a direct indicator of the total number of visible galaxies in the cosmos. By analyzing the change in this average brightness over time, we can infer the universe's expansion rate, which, in a universe with dark energy, will never reach the limit set by the Hubble volume. Any increase in light from distant galaxies would imply the absence of dark energy, whereas any decrease, as it is, suggests the existence of a universal void, which can be viewed as a dark, isolated patch in the fabric of space.

To overcome this limitation, we explore the potential of using large bandwidth symbol extension in Temporal Block Coding, adapting the SEC technique to SE-TC, which leverages the large delay spread to separate overlapping data and coding components in the time domain, thereby enabling high data transmission rates. Since optimizing SE-TCrr is a complex task due to its non-convex nature, we suggest a practical solution by adapting SEC design based on channel conditions, yielding improved performance gains.  To validate our findings, we developed a detailed system model and conducted computer simulations, demonstrating that SE-THrr outperforms both standard TC and SEC techniques in terms of overall error performance.

In this paper, we explore self-supervised methods to rank nodes in large-scale, unlabeled graphs. We investigate two self-supervised approaches: a contrastive method and a predictive method. we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This result is novel as most prior studies on noise cancellation only allowed for the projection of the switching function onto the eigenfunctions orthogonal to the canceling noise. However, in our model, the noise cannot be projected and instead acts as a general distributed source. To overcome this challenge, we employ Carleman estimates to prove the well-posedness of the inverse problem.

Polyps characterized as high-grade dysplasia (HGD) pose a significant risk and necessitate immediate medical attention. In order to accurately identify HGD lesions, the process involves examining tissue samples under a microscope and marking the dysplastic areas. This process relies heavily on the expertise of pathologists and contributes to developing advanced detection systems. To improve system performance, large-scale datasets with precise pathologist annotations are utilized. However, these datasets are limited in size and often contain subjective annotations that can vary in accuracy. This study proposes an alternative approach to HGD characterization, which focuses on analyzing whole slide images rather than smaller image sections. This approach leverages a vast dataset consisting of 11,932 whole slide images from 5,081 patients, collected from three major hospitals in China between 2007 and 2019. The dataset includes whole slide images with varying labels indicating HGD, adenoma, and normal lesions, along with corresponding numerical scores determined by pathologists based on the probability of HGD presence. This study evaluates several data augmentation strategies and conducts experiments to validate the effectiveness of using WSIPolyp-HGD, a newly established benchmark dataset for HGD characterization.

The micro-fracture veins were dated using the U-Pb zircon dating process and found to have formed during the initial stage of Dabie Shan metamorphism at approximately 1300 million years ago.  The micro-fracture veins display significant differences in $\delta^{18}$O and $\delta$D compositions, with larger variations than observed in the surrounding Dabie Shan UHP metamorphic rocks.  The study concludes that the diverse isotopic composition of water in Dabie Shan UHP metamorphic rocks is a result of the interaction between mantle-derived fluids and the metamorphic water, as well as the influence of pre-existing high-quality water sources.

This study presents and assesses different methods for calculating these potentials, focusing on direct and indirect techniques. The direct approach involves using Green's theorem to transform the two-dimensional volume integral into boundary line integrals, which are easier to compute. In contrast, the indirect approach uses separation of variables in a polar coordinate system to obtain the potential over the overlying three-dimensional volume from boundary values. A key finding is that dividing the domain by overlapping sub-regions centered on grid points allows for an accurate and straightforward numerical integration using the Gaussian method. Our research demonstrates that both approaches yield consistent and precise results, but our indirect technique offers a more efficient and user-friendly option.
